clue.text: Military researcher's book, not on, and not out!

parts.note: something switched off is not on
a batter still in is not out, as in cricket

explanation.surface: An exasperated aside about a military scientist's book being neither switched on nor out.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'researcher' stands for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay. BOFFIN is British slang, first used of wartime scientists.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a scientist or technical expert, originally those working on wartime military research.

clue.text: Lie over pubs having abandoned first litre glasses

indicators.note: over in a down clue means turned upside down, so the word reads upwards

parts.note: a fib is a small lie

indicators.note: having abandoned first says the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: a local is one's neighbourhood pub

explanation.surface: A tale about drinking dens that gave up their first litre of beer glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'glasses' looks like the pub's drinkware; it is spectacles.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectacles with lenses split for near and distance vision are a kind of glasses.

clue.text: Overwrought priest with an uncontrollable twitch

parts.note: Fr is the abbreviation for Father, a priest's title
taken as written
a tic is an involuntary muscle spasm

explanation.surface: A stressed-out priest develops a nervous twitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncontrollable' looks like an anagram signal but is part of the description of a tic.
explanation.definitionFit: Wild with anxiety or emotion; both words describe someone in a highly agitated state.

clue.text: Ritzy rhymes of little substance

parts.note: a rhyming phrase that echoes the sound of 'ritzy', meaning tiny or insubstantial

explanation.surface: Posh verses that turn out to be lightweight.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the reduplicated answer rhyme with 'ritzy', and together they mean tiny.
explanation.definitionFit: A childish reduplicated word meaning very small, so of little substance.

clue.text: Nonsense involving singer in West Yorkshire at first

indicators.note: in says the songbird's word sits inside the actress's name

parts.note: Mae West, the American film star, gives her first name
a lark is a songbird, so a singer

indicators.note: at first asks for only the opening letter of the county name

explanation.surface: Some silly business concerning a vocalist performing somewhere in West Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West Yorkshire' reads as one region, but 'West' is Mae West, and only Y comes from Yorkshire. 'involving' merely links definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial word, originally American, for foolish talk or humbug.

clue.text: Father let Edgar fancy becoming king

indicators.note: fancy as a verb means imagine or invent, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A father allowed Edgar to dream of becoming king.
explanation.walkthrough: Edgar was a real English king, adding misdirection. 'becoming' just links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The ninth-century ruler of Wessex who fought the Danes was an English monarch.

clue.text: They oppose one who appears to pray after mass

indicators.note: after says take only what follows the mass letter in the insect's name

parts.note: the praying mantis holds its forelegs as if in prayer
M is the physics symbol for mass

explanation.surface: Opponents who seem pious once mass is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after mass' suggests church; it means the part of MANTIS after its M.
explanation.definitionFit: People against a cause are called the opposition, from the prefix meaning against.

clue.text: Wise guy providing king with zero security

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
no means none at all, zero
a wall gives security or protection

explanation.surface: A smart alec arranging for the king to have no protection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'providing' and 'with' are link words joining the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A smart alec who acts as if he has all the answers is a wise guy.

clue.text: Year that's employed digesting degree course? That's great!

indicators.note: the abbreviation is used to digest, taking the course inside it

parts.note: i.e. is Latin id est, that is
PPE is Philosophy, Politics and Economics, an Oxford degree course

explanation.surface: A year spent studying for a degree, and a cry of delight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's' stands for the Latin abbreviation id est; 'employed digesting' has it swallow the Oxford degree Philosophy, Politics and Economics.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of joy, the same cheer as saying something is great.

clue.text: Assimilate appealing role, and accept amiably

parts.note: to assimilate is to absorb or understand
good can mean attractive or appealing
a part is an actor's role

explanation.surface: An actor absorbs a juicy role and accepts it cheerfully.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay splits the idiom into a verb and a phrase for a desirable role.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means accepting a joke or criticism without offence, with good humour.

clue.text: Bore engaging large workforce, a supporter of raised standards

indicators.note: engaging means taking in or holding, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a fag is British slang for a tedious chore, a bore
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
the staff are the people employed, a workforce

explanation.surface: A tedious person taking on a big workforce, while championing high standards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised standards' sounds like high quality but means flags hoisted up.
explanation.definitionFit: A pole that holds up a flag, so literally it supports a hoisted banner or standard.

clue.text: Cavalry unit's unfortunate time in retreat

indicators.note: in retreat means going backwards, so the letters are read from the end

parts.note: poor can mean unlucky or unfortunate, as in 'poor thing'

explanation.surface: A cavalry unit has a bad time while falling back from battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retreat' fits the military picture but signals reading POOR and T backwards. The 's is 'is', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In the army a subdivision of a cavalry squadron is called this, roughly a platoon of horsemen.

clue.text: Volatile divorcee disappears, potentially facing summons?

indicators.note: disappears says that piece vanishes from the longer word

parts.note: a volatile temperament is easily stirred up, excitable
an ex is a former spouse, a divorcee

explanation.surface: A temperamental ex-wife vanishes and may be served with a court summons.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: someone liable to be cited is summoned, so 'potentially facing summons' describes them; the question mark flags the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: To cite someone is to summon them to court, so a person who could be cited may face a summons.

clue.text: Subjugate East European held captive in quarters

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation for east

indicators.note: held captive in says one piece is enclosed by the other

parts.note: the compass points are quarters; here north and east, N and E
a Slav is a person from eastern Europe

explanation.surface: Conquer by locking an Eastern European prisoner in a cell block.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quarters' suggests lodgings but gives two compass points, N and E, which surround SLAV.
explanation.definitionFit: To subjugate a people is to bring them under control, making them into slaves.

clue.text: Lawful to petition for? Not so

indicators.note: Not says the following word is to be left out of the longer one

parts.note: to solicit something is to petition or ask for it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Is it legal to petition for something? Apparently not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not so' reads as a denial, but tells you to remove SO from the front of SOLICIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal word for permitted by law, the opposite of illicit.

clue.text: Part of Brazil in which, briefly, you have it?

definitions.meaning: a brazil is a nut, and its hard outer case is part of it

definitions.text: in which, briefly, you have it?
definitions.meaning: the idiom 'in a ...' means summed up briefly

explanation.surface: A puzzle about a region of the South American country where everything is summed up.
explanation.walkthrough: Brazil looks like the country, but it is the brazil nut; the capital is just the clue's opening word.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard casing of a nut is part of it, and the phrase 'in a ...' means put very concisely.

clue.text: Note received by lady's man beginning to eat rabbit, say

indicators.note: received by puts the note directly after the lady's word

parts.note: her is the possessive pronoun for a lady
B is a note of the musical scale
Ivor is a man's name

indicators.note: beginning to asks for the first letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A man receives a note from a lady while starting to eat rabbit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rabbit, say' looks like food; 'say' marks it as an example of a plant-eater.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbit is an example of an animal that eats only plants.

clue.text: Neat one is red, perhaps: it produces rust

parts.note: neat is an old word for cattle, of which an ox is one
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: perhaps hints the letters may be arranged otherwise

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tidy one is red, maybe, as it makes rust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' looks like tidy; it is an archaic word for cattle, giving OX.
explanation.definitionFit: Rust forms when oxygen combines with iron, so an agent that does this makes rust.

clue.text: Sweetheart offering boy nothing after a year

indicators.note: after places the nil score behind the year

parts.note: a lad is a boy
love means nil, a score of nothing in tennis

explanation.surface: A sweetheart, a boy who has offered no love once a year has passed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nothing' suggests a cold shoulder; it is the tennis score LOVE.
explanation.definitionFit: A beloved woman, an old-fashioned word for a sweetheart or girlfriend.

clue.text: Zeppelin's entitlement as next in line, so to speak

parts.note: heirship is the right of inheritance belonging to an heir

explanation.surface: A Zeppelin's claim to be next in the succession.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'Zeppelin' stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Zeppelins were German rigid dirigibles, a type of lighter-than-air craft.

clue.text: Some prefer a Dixieland number as basis

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Jazz fans who like New Orleans style pick a number from it as their foundation.
explanation.definitionFit: In mathematics, the base of a number system, such as ten for decimal, is the number serving as its basis.

clue.text: Canine predators identified by duke during travels

parts.note: in can mean during, as in 'in the night'
goes means moves or travels

explanation.surface: Wild dogs spotted by a duke on his journeys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'identified by' is just a link phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Australian wild dogs that hunt prey are wild canines.

clue.text: Queasiness of Greek character traversing a mass of water

parts.note: nu is a letter of the Greek alphabet
taken as written
a sea is a large body of water

explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' suggests a person; it is a letter of the alphabet.

clue.text: What a trader may run a sporting venue?

parts.note: a ground is a stadium or pitch where sport is played

clue.text: Pigment from river talked of in Bow?

clue.text: Held sway, acquiescent son having withdrawn

parts.note: resigned means accepting something unwelcome without protest, acquiescent

clue.text: Indian address one book has got wrong

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

clue.text: An old American keeping a register is comparable

taken as written

clue.text: How Hook appeared, having one to begin with
